item.title: Baghdad confirms attack on Saudi pipeline came from Iraq
item.description:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States is again fighting a major war in the Middle East. Drop Site’s Ryan Grim and Murtaza Hussain speak with Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at Johns Hopkins SAIS and a former senior adviser in the Obama administration, and Rob Malley, a senior fellow at Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs, former U.S. special envoy for Iran, longtime Middle East peace negotiator, and head of the Middle East program at the International Crisis Group. The conversation covers Ansarallah’s advance in Yemen, the battle over the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and the US duel strategies of economic pressure, the future of U.S. military bases in the Gulf, the collapse of the JCPOA, Iran’s nuclear calculations, and whether Washington has learned the lessons of Iraq, Afghanistan and the broader post-9/11 wars. item.title: US court rejects Trump’s emergency order keeping Michigan coal plant open
item.description:
The Department of Energy overstepped when it ordered an aging coal-fired power plant in Michigan to stay open past its planned retirement date last year, a federal court ruled on Friday. The J.H Campbell plant is one of seven fossil fuel plants around the country that the Trump administration has forced to stay in operation, despite the pollution they cause and the enormous costs of keeping them online. Just before it was about to close last May, Trump’s Energy Department invoked short-term emergency powers under the Federal Power Act to keep the 64-year-old plant running, arguing that the threat of outages, along with the need for more energy to power data centers, constituted an emergency. item.title: OPINION: 25 years on, a nation still mourns
item.description:
When the alerts came on September 11, 2001 , I first made sure my kids were safe and then headed to home base, which for me was that concrete lifesaver – Bellevue Hospital. I helped empty the hospital where I had trained, triaging patients to other facilities in preparation for World Trade Center survivors. Then we waited for hours for survivors who never came. A few days later, I visited the disaster site, and when I arrived, I was handed an N95 mask. I made my way through the rubble, very aware that I was in the presence of potentially toxic chemicals and fumes. It was a bright, sunny day, but there was still a film in the air. With all due respect to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is claiming the public was lied to and has released 170,000 documents related to the attacks to supposedly verify a cover-up, I have a simple response. item.title: Remember: The "S" in "Artificial Intelligence" Stands for "Safety"
item.description:
There are only a handful of moments in American life that split time into before and after—where you were when John F. Kennedy was assassinated, when the Challenger exploded, when the Twin Towers fell. September 11, 2001, was one of those moments. To mark the 25th anniversary, we asked a range of people who were at Ground Zero, at the Pentagon, or hundreds of miles away that day to tell us about what they experienced and how they think Americans should remember it today. —The Editors Jennifer Altman, a New York photojournalist, was driving to an assignment in Brooklyn.
